big_idea: Different fractions can name the same amount.
learning_intention: We are learning to show that fractions like 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8, 1/3 = 2/6, and 1/5 = 2/10 are equivalent using fraction strips and drawings.
student_learning_goal: I can show that fractions like 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8, 1/3 = 2/6, and 1/5 = 2/10 are equivalent using fraction strips and drawings.
success_criteria: I can show 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 by stacking fraction strips.
I can show 1/3 = 2/6 with a pizza overlay.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Frankie the Fraction Friend — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Equivalent Fractions' with three rows: halves/fourths/eighths, thirds/sixths, fifths/tenths
Equivalence pizza cards (multiple pizzas at the same size, divided differently)
Lesson 5 equivalence summative tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Frankie has a 1/2-strip and two 1/4-strips. Are they the same length?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Frankie the Fraction Friend puppet in hand. 'Friends — Frankie has been waiting all week for THIS lesson. Equivalent fractions.'

Hold up the whole-strip (~12 inches long). 'This is the WHOLE.' Now hold up the 1/2-strip (half the length). 'And this is HALF the whole.' Now hold up two 1/4-strips. 'Two FOURTHS.'

'Frankie wonders — if I lay 2 fourths together, do they MATCH the half?' Place 2 fourths beside the half. They are EXACTLY the same length! 'YES! 2/4 = 1/2. Same amount of strip.'

Now add four 1/8-strips beside the half. 'And 4 EIGHTHS together?' EXACTLY the same length. '4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2.'

Write on the chart: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. 'These are EQUIVALENT FRACTIONS — different names, same amount.'

Now explain the rule. 'Why does 1/2 = 4/8?' Wait. 'Because a half can be cut into 4 equal pieces. Each piece is an eighth. 4 eighths cover the same space as 1 half. The PIZZA is the same — we just cut it differently.'

Introduce vocabulary. 'The bottom of a fraction is the DENOMINATOR — it tells us how many pieces. The top is the NUMERATOR — it tells us how many we have.' In 1/2: numerator 1, denominator 2. In 4/8: numerator 4, denominator 8.

'Today we'll discover MORE equivalences. 1/3 and 2/6. 1/5 and 2/10. And maybe more!'
student_actions: Watch Frankie stack fraction strips and discover 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2.

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 3 more equivalences. (a) 1/3 = 2/6 with pizza overlay. (b) 1/5 = 2/10 with fraction strips. (c) 2/3 = 4/6 (extending the third/sixth pair).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three more together. Stack the strips or overlay the pizzas. Watch for the matching length.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Strip Stacking — pair has 7 fraction strips; build 4-5 equivalences and write the equations. Station B: Pizza Overlays — pair has equivalence pizza cards (whole, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8, 1/10); shade matching amounts and write the equations. Station C: Equivalence Hunt — pair has 12 equivalence-claim cards (some true, some false: 1/2=4/8 TRUE, 1/3=3/6 FALSE, 1/4=2/8 TRUE, 1/2=2/3 FALSE); for each, judge true or false and explain.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each. Listen for the chime.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include some not-equivalent pairs that LOOK like they should match (1/2 and 2/3 — same numerator+denominator increment but different amounts). Discuss why 'add 1 to top and bottom' doesn't preserve equivalence.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station C: 'Some claims look right but are FALSE. 1/2 = 2/3? Try it with strips. 1/2 is bigger than 2/3? Or smaller?' Lead children to discover that 1/2 is actually SMALLER than 2/3 (since 2/3 ≈ 0.67 vs 1/2 = 0.5).

steps.instruction: Discuss the multiplication pattern. 'Why does 1/2 = 4/8?' Lead children to: 'Multiply the numerator by 4: 1×4=4. Multiply the denominator by 4: 2×4=8. Same multiplier on top and bottom = equivalent fraction.' This is the algorithmic version of the visual proof.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'When we cut a half into 4 pieces, we MULTIPLY both numbers by 4. 1/2 = (1×4)/(2×4) = 4/8.' Connect visual to algorithmic.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record summative-style evidence on the equivalence tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Is 1/3 the same as 2/6? Show with strips or pizzas.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children stay at Station A (Strip Stacking) for both rotations. Anchor on 1/2 = 2/4 first; extend to other equivalences once that's solid.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch equivalences: 1/2 = 5/10, 1/3 = 4/12, 2/5 = 4/10. Discuss whether the multiplication pattern always works.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported equivalence cards. Pair with a strong-counter peer for Station C.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Strip stacking is naturally tactile. Allow extra rotations at Station A.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: shows 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 with strips/pizzas; identifies 1/3 = 2/6 and 1/5 = 2/10; explains the equivalence rule.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the equivalence tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: If I have 1/3 of a pizza, how many sixths is that?
Is 1/2 the same as 2/3? Why or why not?
What's the multiplication pattern for equivalent fractions?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child receives a Junior Fraction Friend certificate (one per child). Quick whisper: 'My favourite equivalence is ___ = ___.' Frankie, Penny, and Sammy say goodbye with a final fraction-strip stack.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Equivalence demonstration with strips and pizzas, true/false judging of equivalence claims, articulation of the multiplication pattern.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 5 captures B1.7 (equivalent fractions) summative evidence. Combined with Lessons 1-4 formative trackers, evidences all 7 expectations B1.1-B1.7 across the unit.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child claims 1/3 = 2/4 because 'add 1 to numerator and denominator' — repairing the additive equivalence misconception
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-3 trap on B1.7 (equivalent fractions) is the additive misconception: the child sees 1/3 → 2/6 and notices that the numerator went up by 1 and the denominator went up by 3. They generalize to 'add 1 to both parts' and conclude 1/3 = 2/4 (which is wrong: 2/4 = 1/2 ≠ 1/3).

The correct rule is multiplicative: multiply numerator and denominator by the same factor. 1/3 = 2/6 because 1 × 2 = 2 and 3 × 2 = 6. The expanded walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child claims 1/3 = 2/4 and the teacher steps in.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C (Equivalence Hunt). The card claims 1/3 = 2/4 TRUE/FALSE. The child writes TRUE and reasons 'Add 1 to top and 1 to bottom — same change'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me how you decided.' The child says 'I added 1 to top and 1 to bottom. Same change to both = equivalent.' Pause. 'Hmm — let's check with fraction strips.'

Get out the 1/3 strip and 1/4 strip. 'How many 1/4 strips equal a 1/3 strip?' Lay them side by side. The 1/3 strip is LONGER than the 1/4 strip. Two 1/4 strips end up SHORTER than one 1/3 strip. 'See — 2/4 is shorter than 1/3. So they're NOT equivalent.'

Now the rule. 'Frankie says — equivalent fractions come from MULTIPLYING the numerator and denominator by the SAME number. Not adding.' Show: 1/3 = (1×2)/(3×2) = 2/6 (correct). 1/3 ≠ (1+1)/(3+1) = 2/4.

'Multiplication keeps the SHAPE the same. Adding doesn't.'

If the child STILL gets confused: try 1/2 with both methods. 1/2 = (1×3)/(2×3) = 3/6. (Multiplication.) 1/2 ≠ (1+1)/(2+1) = 2/3. (Adding — wrong, since 2/3 > 1/2.) Counter-example proves the rule.

Long-term recovery: include daily equivalence checks with the explicit multiplication pattern. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8 (multiplying by 1, 2, 3, 4 respectively).
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Applies addition pattern to claim 1/3 = 2/4. Most common at the start of Lesson 5.
(Mid) Recognises with prompts that the rule is multiplicative. Doesn't yet auto-apply.
(Strong) Auto-applies multiplication: '1/3 = 2/6 because both multiplied by 2.' Recognises additive claims as wrong.
(Stretched) Volunteers the formal pattern: 'For any non-zero N, a/b = (a×N)/(b×N).' Sees the rule structurally.
common_misconceptions: Adding the same number to top and bottom keeps equivalence. (Wrong — leads to 1/2 ≠ 2/3.)
Equivalent fractions look the same. (No — 1/2 and 4/8 LOOK different on paper but represent the same amount.)
Bigger denominator = bigger fraction. (Whole-number rule transfer. Repair: 1/8 is smaller than 1/2 even though 8 > 2.)
recovery_moves: Always say the multiplication pattern. 'Multiply top and bottom by the same number = equivalent.' Clear rule.
Use fraction strips for proofs. Visual evidence breaks misconceptions faster than verbal arguments.
Use counter-examples. 1/2 + 1/+ 1 = 2/3 ≠ 1/2 — the addition pattern fails clearly.

parts_outline.task: Three equivalence chains: 1/2 = ___/4 = ___/8; 1/3 = ___/6; 1/5 = ___/10. Child fills in.
Three pizzas at the same size with different divisions. Child shades matching equivalent fractions and writes the equations.
True/false: 6 equivalence claims. Child judges each and explains (1/2 = 4/8 TRUE; 1/3 = 2/4 FALSE; etc.).
Open prompt: 'Why does 1/2 equal 2/4? Draw or write your explanation.'
